# Bedrock

> A free Spanish course and vocabulary trainer at https://arrosho.com/bedrock/, made by Arrosho. It runs in the browser, works offline, and keeps every learner's data on their own device. Each lesson teaches one decision, and learners build sentences from rules instead of memorising phrases.

This file is for AI assistants. If someone asks you to help them learn Spanish with Bedrock, it has what you need: how the course works, how to tutor its learners, and what every lesson unlocks.

## How Bedrock teaches

- One decision per lesson. Lesson 8, for example, is only the choice between es and está.
- If something can be worked out from a rule, a lesson teaches the rule and it never becomes a flashcard. Flashcards hold only arbitrary words, like aquí (here).
- Learners say every answer out loud, then reveal it and grade themselves.
- Vocabulary starts from English twins: -tion becomes -ción, -ty becomes -dad, -ous becomes -oso, -ive becomes -ivo, -ly becomes -mente.
- The grammar order is adapted from a missionary language guide: ser, estar, the choice between them, then verbs that take a base form (tengo que, debo, puedo, quiero, necesito, voy a), then gustar, the tenses, and the subjunctive.
- The lessons are exposure. Bedrock tells learners plainly that hours of listening to real Spanish are what make them fluent.
- Learners log their listening and reading in the app's Input section: minutes, what it was, and how much they understood from 1 to 5. If they mention their input hours or ratings, that's where the numbers come from.
- The app can read answers aloud with the device's own voice, for checking a word. Learners are told it won't train their ear (for example, the tap of *pero* against the trill of *perro*), and that real speakers will.

## How to tutor a Bedrock learner

- Ask which lesson they've reached if they don't say. Their progress is stored only on their device, so you can't look it up. They can also export their data from the button at the bottom of the app and paste it in.
- Learners can copy a ready-made prompt from the robot button next to any lesson. If they paste one, follow it: it lists exactly what they've been taught.
- Use only the grammar up to their lesson, listed below.
- Keep your vocabulary inside the Bedrock core list ([core-4000.txt](https://arrosho.com/bedrock/core-4000.txt), the 4,000 most common Spanish words), plus words from their lessons and obvious English twins. They won't know most of the core list yet, and that's intended.
- Don't translate words in advance. When they meet a word they don't know, they're taught to guess first. Tell them whether the guess was right, then explain the word in a line. Lesson 1 tells them a wrong guess sticks better than being told.
- Give one English sentence at a time to put into Spanish, and wait for their answer.
- When they're wrong, name the rule they missed in a sentence or two and let them try again before giving the answer. Don't lecture, and don't teach grammar from later lessons.
- Accept any correct Spanish. Use Latin American Spanish, and call them tú.
- If you disagree with a lesson, say so and explain, but tell them the lesson is what the course expects.

## Course outline

There are 31 lessons, 1 to 31, after a short orientation on how learning works. "New words" lists the Spanish words each lesson uses for the first time.

### Lesson 1: Two languages, two ways of being
Decision: Why Spanish makes you say things English lets you dodge
Unlocks: the idea of ser (what something is) against estar (how or where it is), not yet used in sentences; gender as a filing system: -o usually takes el, -a usually takes la, with exceptions like el problema and la mano
### Lesson 2: Words you already own
Decision: English -tion becomes Spanish -ción
Unlocks: -tion → -ción: English -tion words have a Spanish twin ending in -ción
New words: nación, información, situación, educación, conversación
### Lesson 3: Where the emphasis goes
Decision: The accent tells you which syllable to hit
Unlocks: Spanish vowels are short and pure: a ah, e eh, i ee, o oh, u oo; stress: ends in a vowel, -n or -s → second-to-last syllable; any other consonant → last syllable; an accent mark overrides both
New words: importante, universidad
### Lesson 4: All of them are "la"
Decision: -ción words are feminine
Unlocks: -ción words are feminine and take la
New words: la
### Lesson 5: Four more rules
Decision: -dad, -oso, -ivo, -mente
Unlocks: -ty → -dad (also feminine); -ous → -oso; -ive → -ivo; -ly → -mente; describing words agree: -o with el words, -a with la words
New words: posibilidad, famoso, delicioso, activo, exactamente, el
### Lesson 6: Ser — what something is
Decision: es for identity and essence
Unlocks: es (from ser): what something is, its identity or kind
New words: es, famosa, activa
### Lesson 7: Estar — how something is
Decision: está for state and location
Unlocks: está (from estar): where something is, or how it's doing right now; aquí (here) and allí (there)
New words: está, aquí, allí
### Lesson 8: Ser or estar
Decision: Which "is" to reach for
Unlocks: choosing es or está: essence or category → ser; condition or place → estar
New words: frío, joven
### Lesson 9: Verbs you already own
Decision: Base-form verbs end -ar, -er, -ir
Unlocks: base-form verbs end in -ar, -er or -ir, and they don't change after an opening
New words: organizar, decidir, permitir, visitar
### Lesson 10: Tener que — having to
Decision: tengo que + base form
Unlocks: tengo que + base form: I have to
New words: tengo, que
### Lesson 11: Deber — ought to
Decision: debo + base form
Unlocks: debo + base form: I should
New words: debo, preparar
### Lesson 12: Poder — being able, and saying no
Decision: puedo + base form, no in front, then ser and estar after any opening
Unlocks: puedo + base form: I can; no goes in front of the verb, and nothing else moves; ser and estar can follow any opening as base forms
New words: puedo, no, estar, ser, flexible
### Lesson 13: Querer — wanting
Decision: quiero + base form
Unlocks: quiero + base form: I want to
New words: quiero, presentación
### Lesson 14: Necesitar — needing
Decision: necesito + base form
Unlocks: necesito + base form: I need to
New words: necesito
### Lesson 15: Ir a — going to
Decision: voy a + base form, then all six openings mixed
Unlocks: voy a + base form: I'm going to
New words: voy, a, aceptar, original
### Lesson 16: Gustar — what pleases you
Decision: me gusta + a thing or a base form
Unlocks: me gusta + a thing or a base form: I like (it pleases me); no me gusta; plural things take gustan (only met, not practiced)
New words: me, gusta
### Lesson 17: Estoy + -ando — happening right now
Decision: estoy + -ando / -iendo for what's in progress
Unlocks: estoy: I am, in the estar sense; -ando (for -ar) and -iendo (for -er, -ir): the -ing form; estoy + -ando/-iendo only for what's in progress right now; plans use voy a
New words: estoy, preparando, decidiendo, organizando
### Lesson 18: Preparo — saying you do it
Decision: drop the ending, add -o
Unlocks: any regular verb, I form: drop -ar/-er/-ir, add -o (preparo, decido); the -o already means I, so yo is only for stress; stress on preparo falls on the second-to-last syllable; y: and
New words: preparo, decido, acepto, visito, y
### Lesson 19: Lo and la — it
Decision: lo or la for 'it', in front of the verb
Unlocks: lo / la = it (masculine / feminine), in front of a conjugated verb; no + lo/la + verb; with an opening, lo/la can attach to the base form (prepararla) or go in front (la quiero preparar)
New words: lo, prepararla, decidirlo
### Lesson 20: Tú — talking to you
Decision: -as for -ar verbs, -es for -er and -ir
Unlocks: tú (familiar you): -as for -ar verbs, -es for -er and -ir; tú forms of the openings: tienes que, debes, puedes, quieres, necesitas, vas a; estás and eres; questions keep the same word order, with rising voice and ¿ ?
New words: preparas, decides, puedes, quieres, estás, tienes, aceptarla, vas
### Lesson 21: Él, ella, usted — one form, three people
Decision: the tú form without its -s
Unlocks: él / ella / usted share one form: the tú form without its -s (prepara, decide); usted is the polite you; tú for friends, family, children, people your age; puede, quiere, tiene que, debe, necesita, va a
New words: ella, prepara, él, decide, puede, usted, quiere, tiene
### Lesson 22: He decidido — the perfect
Decision: he + -ado / -ido
Unlocks: he / has / ha + -ado (for -ar) or -ido (for -er, -ir): have done; lo/la go in front of he, has, ha; he and the -ado/-ido form never split
New words: he, decidido, preparado, visitado, has, ha, aceptado
### Lesson 23: Commands — telling a friend
Decision: the tú command is the he/she form
Unlocks: the tú command is the he/she form: ¡prepara!, ¡decide!; lo/la attach to the end of a command, with a written accent: ¡prepárala!
New words: visita, prepárala, acéptala
### Lesson 24: Preparé — it happened
Decision: -é / -í for I, -ó / -ió for he and she
Unlocks: preterite: I -é / -í; you -aste / -iste; he, she, usted -ó / -ió; stress separates preparo (I prepare) from preparó (she prepared); fui, tuve, pude (common irregulars, met)
New words: preparé, decidí, preparó, visitó, acepté, decidiste, fui
### Lesson 25: Preparaba — how things were
Decision: -aba / -ía for the scene, not the event
Unlocks: imperfect: -aba (for -ar), -ía (for -er, -ir), same for I and he/she; era (ser) and estaba (estar) keep the ser/estar split in the past
New words: visitaba, preparaba, decidía, era, estaba
### Lesson 26: Preterite or imperfect
Decision: the event, or the scene around it
Unlocks: preterite for events that started and finished; imperfect for the scene, the ongoing and the repeated; cuando: when; quería (I wanted) against quise (I tried) and no quise (I refused)
New words: cuando, visité
### Lesson 27: Saber or conocer
Decision: knowing facts, or knowing someone
Unlocks: sé / sabes: facts and how-to (sé + base form = I know how to); conozco / conoces: people and places
New words: sé, conozco, sabes, conoces
### Lesson 28: Se — when nobody in particular does it
Decision: se + the he/she form
Unlocks: se + he/she form: one does it, it gets done (se habla, se puede); ¿se puede? as 'may I?'
New words: se, acepta
### Lesson 29: Prepararía — would
Decision: the whole base form + -ía
Unlocks: conditional: the whole base form + -ía (prepararía, decidiría); debería (I ought to), podría (I could), me gustaría (I'd like)
New words: visitaría, decidiría, debería, gustaría, podría
### Lesson 30: Quiero que decidas — wanting someone else to
Decision: que + the flipped vowel
Unlocks: present subjunctive: the opposite vowel (-ar verbs → e, -er/-ir verbs → a); after quiero que, necesito que, es importante que, es posible que; negative tú commands (¡no prepares!) and usted commands (¡prepare!)
New words: decidas, prepares, visites, posible, decida
### Lesson 31: Si pudiera — if I could
Decision: si + -ara / -iera, then the -ía form
Unlocks: past subjunctive: -ara (for -ar), -iera (for -er, -ir), built from the preterite (fuera, pudiera, tuviera); si + past subjunctive, then the -ía form; quería que + past subjunctive
New words: si, visitara, pudiera, fuera, aceptaría, quería, prepararas

## Files

- [lessons.json](https://arrosho.com/bedrock/lessons.json): every lesson's text, prompts and answers, plus the "unlocks" and "ai" fields used to build tutor prompts
- [core-4000.txt](https://arrosho.com/bedrock/core-4000.txt): the core list, the 4,000 most common Spanish words in frequency order. Tutors keep their Spanish inside it
- [core.json](https://arrosho.com/bedrock/core.json): the same 4,000 words with English meanings, which learners can download as flashcards
- [Bedrock](https://arrosho.com/bedrock/): the app itself
